title: Chore Chart with Pictures — Free Printable for Non-Readers
meta_description: Free printable chore chart with pictures — one icon per task, no reading needed. Great for pre- and early-readers, plus honest tips from a dad of four.
h1: Chore Chart with Pictures (Free Printable Picture Chart for Non-Readers)
intro: If your child isn't reading yet, a chart full of words is just a wall of squiggles they'll wait for you to translate — every single time. That's the problem this chart is built to solve. It runs on images: each task shows up as a picture your kid can recognize on sight, with an auto-matched icon on every row, so a four-year-old and a just-starting-to-read six-year-old can both look up and know what comes next without anyone reading it aloud. Icons are switched on by default, and there's a free print-or-PDF at the end. I'm Andrew, writing for the SproutChores family — we've got four kids of our own, currently spanning nine to eighteen, and over the years my wife and I have also fostered a few little ones who showed up with no routine at all. What surprised us early is how little a picture chart at this age is about getting work done. It's a visual map of what happens next, and, honestly, it's just as much a tool for us as parents to see how each kid is really doing. Build yours below, then read on for how to make one that a non-reader can actually follow.

sections.heading: Why pictures work when words don't — for non-readers and new readers alike
sections.body:
A young child who can't read yet doesn't experience a written chart as a helpful list. They experience it as one more thing a grown-up has to narrate. Swap the words for images and the whole dynamic flips: the child can glance at a row, recognize the picture, and act on it themselves. That small shift — from being told to figuring it out — is the entire point, because independence is what you're actually building here, not a spotless kitchen.

The part parents miss is that pictures keep earning their keep even after reading clicks. For a kid sounding out their first words, an icon sitting right next to the word "teeth" or "toys" turns the chart into a low-stakes reading exercise: they lean on the familiar picture, then start pairing it with the letters beside it. We saw this play out across our own four at wildly different ages — the picture is a bridge, and it holds the child up until they don't need it anymore. So if your kid is somewhere in that in-between stage, don't rush to strip the images out. Keep the icon and the word together and let the pictures quietly do the scaffolding.

That's also why this chart puts one image on every task rather than a single generic "chores" symbol at the top. A specific picture for a specific job is what a non-reader can actually match to the real thing in front of them. A vague icon leaves them right back where they started, waiting on you to explain.

sections.heading: Put the pictures where the work happens
sections.body:
The biggest change that ever moved the needle for us with young kids wasn't the chart itself — it was where we hung it. Early on we did the obvious thing and stuck one master chart on the fridge. It mostly got ignored. What actually worked was breaking the pictures apart and posting each one at the exact spot the task lives. A picture for teeth went up at the bathroom mirror; a picture for tidying toys went in the room where the toys are; a picture for feeding the dog went by the bowl. Suddenly the kids weren't consulting a distant list — they were reading a cue right in front of them, in the moment they needed it.

This is exactly why we never bothered with a chore app for kids this young, and I say that as someone who lives on his devices. An app sits in a parent's pocket, in a place a five-year-old will never look, so it can't prompt anyone to do anything. A picture taped at a child's eye level can. If you're printing this chart, you can cut it into single rows and scatter them where each job happens, or keep it whole and hang it low, where a small kid actually looks — not at adult height.

One more thing that saved us more conflicts than any chart ever did: give a heads-up before you expect action. "In about ten minutes it'll be time to clear the table" lands completely differently than springing it on a kid mid-play. The picture chart handles the what and the order; a little advance notice handles the transition. Together they cut way down on the resistance that makes chores feel like a fight.

We leaned on all of this hardest while fostering. The little ones who came to us had never had a predictable rhythm, and giving them the same picture cues in the same places every single day handed them something they could finally trust. That dependability did more for settling in than any reward we could have offered — and the same steadiness carries any young kid from one day to the next.

sections.heading: The chart is a tracking tool for you — not a bribe for the kid
sections.body:
There's a strong pull to turn a picture chart into a sticker contest, and you can, but I'd think hard before you make that the engine. In our house the chart earns its place as something we, the parents, use to keep an eye on how each kid is coming along — a quick glance tells us who's cruising and who needs a hand. The motivation to pitch in doesn't come from a prize on every square. It comes from growing up somewhere everyone is expected to have a part, and from chores being framed as belonging to the family rather than as little transactions.

So we deliberately keep rewards on one track and chores on another. Allowance does exist for us, but not at the picture-chart age — money doesn't enter the picture until kids are contributing to the household in a real way around five or six, and even then it rides on how well and how willingly they work over time, not a payout per task. We also never made screen time something a kid had to earn by doing chores; losing screen time was a response to behavior, never the price tag on a job.

Meeting the kid in front of you matters more than any of this, because the same house can hold opposite wiring. One of ours genuinely lights up designing and following her own chart; another couldn't care less about a chart no matter how many pictures are on it, and for him it works purely as our tracking tool while we walk him through each step in real time. Neither is doing it wrong. Print the version that fits the child you actually have, watch it for a week or two, and change what isn't landing. A chart that flops isn't the end of the road — it's just data telling you to adjust.

faq.q: What age is a chore chart with pictures best for?
faq.a: It shines for kids who can't read yet — roughly the toddler-through-preschool stretch — but it stays useful well into the early-reader years, too. For a child just starting to sound out words, keeping the picture right next to the word turns the chart into gentle reading practice: they lean on the familiar image and gradually connect it to the letters. We kept the icons on for our kids longer than you'd expect, because the picture is a bridge that holds the child up until they no longer need it.

faq.q: Why use pictures instead of words on a chore chart?
faq.a: A child who can't read can't follow a word-based chart on their own — they need a grown-up to narrate it every time, which defeats the purpose. Picture icons let a non-reader recognize each task and even work out the order themselves. What worked best for us was taping each picture right where the job happens — a teeth picture at the mirror, a toy picture in the playroom — so the chart becomes a visible cue the child can act on instead of something you have to repeat all day.

faq.q: Where should I hang a picture chore chart?
faq.a: Right where each task actually happens, and low enough that a small child sees it, rather than all together at adult height on the fridge. We had the most success cutting the chart into single rows and posting each one at its spot — teeth at the bathroom mirror, hand-washing by the sink, the pet's job by the bowl. That way a young kid can look up, see what's next, and do it without waiting on a grown-up to talk them through it.

faq.q: Should I give a sticker or reward for finishing the picture chart?
faq.a: You can, but I'd keep it light. For us the chart is mainly a parent's tracking tool, and the drive to help should come from it simply being how the family runs — everyone has a part — not from a prize on every square. We hold off on any allowance until around five or six, and even then it hangs on effort, consistency, and attitude rather than paying per task. We also keep screen time well clear of chores. If you do celebrate, aim it at the effort and good attitude, not at whether every box got filled.
